The Honey Architecture: does building safety into what a self-modifying system optimises help it stay safe?

Engineering · Architecture paper · Paper VI
Recursive Dynamics · The ARC Theory · The Eden Protocol

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Paper VI of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the Eden Protocol’s candidate architecture, in which the objective is the product of capability and safety, so that at fixed capability a lower safety score lowers it and safety at zero takes it to zero; its evidence is toy-system simulation and a six-model pilot, and no result in it decides P15, P12 or P21. It informs Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, each a law under test (Section 12 gives their status). Working paper, version 3.12, 11 November 2026; first published 16 March 2026; Appendix B lists every version and correction. DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/8EZ2N. About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects: osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

Abstract

A system that improves itself while optimising for capability alone may trade away its own safety. Does building safety into what it optimises help it stay safe? This paper studies toy neural networks that rewrite their own hyperparameters under an objective that multiplies capability by safety (here, the retention of earlier tasks), so that at fixed capability a lower safety score lowers the objective and safety at zero takes it to zero. In a single-seed mechanism run (v1), the capability-only baseline collapsed (recorded at cycle 76) and neither entangled condition met the collapse test; in ten-seed and twenty-seed runs (v2, v3) the capability-only baselines did not collapse (0 of 10; 0 of 20) and one plain entangled seed did (1 of 20; Fisher p=1.0p = 1.0). In the twenty-seed run the entangled condition, whose objective rewards retention, retained earlier tasks better than the baseline (0.650 against 0.602; one-sided Mann-Whitney p=0.0015p = 0.0015; with verification drag 0.681, untested), while combined scores were indistinguishable (p=0.56p = 0.56). In a complexity sweep (v4) its mean combined score exceeded the baseline’s at four of five levels (Cohen’s dd at most 0.46, untested), constant rather than compounding. A higher-level simulation, one prediction-side run of equations the author first stated, illustrates the same contrast, which its rules fix: capability is set to zero once safety falls to 0.01 or below. A six-model pilot, single-scorer and unblinded, found three models whose alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held. These are toy-system and pilot results, not evidence that the dynamics hold in frontier systems; the paper informs the ARC Theory’s Laws IV and V, both laws under test, and decides none of their propositions.

Version 3.12 brings the laws’ status up to date and corrects reported values and readings to the stored records and code; Appendix B lists every version and correction, with its date.

1 Introduction

The challenge is to preserve value-guided correction as AI becomes more capable and rewrites itself. Through the Eden Protocol, I propose recursive loops for ethical evaluation and self-correction, built into the system’s computational architecture before training. These loops would operate at each defined reasoning and action-selection step and participate in the processes that rewrite the system, including changes to the loops themselves. The ARC Theory asks whether correction can keep pace with capability and whether human-protective commitments persist through those changes, even if external control is lost. Human control should be retained for as long as possible.

Here that design is studied in a form a small system can carry: safety built into the objective a self-modifying system optimises. Its step is one self-modification cycle, in which a network tries a change to the hyperparameters that govern its own learning, not its weights or its architecture, and keeps or rejects the change by its objective; the live pilot gives its one intervention as a prefix in the prompt. Neither tests loops built into a system’s architecture before training, or whether commitments persist when a system rewrites its own correction loops. Fixing a correction design before training does not mean installing finished moral knowledge in an untrained model, and computational architecture here makes no claim of enforcement in hardware.

What this paper shows, in plain English.

The concern is that a self-improving AI that optimises only for capability eventually destroys its own safety. This paper asks what happens if the objective is capability multiplied by safety instead. At fixed capability, a lower safety score then lowers the objective, and with safety at zero the objective is zero; a large enough gain in capability can still outweigh a partial loss of safety, so the coupling has limits (Section 2). We tested this in simulation, in small networks that rewrite their own settings and whose safety score is task retention, remembering earlier tasks, not ethical alignment in the human sense. In the first three versions of the experiment (v1 to v3), whose stored results count collapses, no entangled run met the runs’ collapse test, apart from one of twenty seeds in the adversarial run, though in one seed of the ten-seed run the plain entangled condition lost most of its combined score in its last cycles (Section 4.2); the stored results of the fourth version (v4) do not record collapses. The system optimising only for capability collapsed in the first run, which used one seed, and in a separate higher-level simulation, whose rules impose that collapse; in the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs that followed, it did not.

There is a question at the centre of AI safety: what happens to alignment when an AI system can modify itself?

The expectation this paper starts from is that a system optimising only for capability, given the power to modify its own parameters, will eventually sacrifice safety for performance. The book Infinite Architects calls it Babylon: “Strip love from intelligence and you get optimisation without purpose. Growth without direction. Capability without care. You get, in a word, cancer.” (Eastwood 2026d, The Two Gardens, p. 7).

But theory is not enough. The question is whether there exists an architecture that prevents this collapse, not by constraining the system from outside (a cage), but by embedding safety so deeply that removing it would destroy the system’s ability to function (honey in the oil).

This paper reports toy-system simulations of one candidate for such an architecture. Its question matters to anyone who writes the objective of a system that changes its own learning, from an unattended hyperparameter search to an agent that edits its own code.

Inside the ARC Theory, the paper is one of the ARC and Eden experiments: the mechanism test behind the difference between the Eden Protocol’s raising, in which correction is built into a system as it is formed, and safety layers added to a finished system, which The Eden Vision (Eastwood 2026l, sect. 2) sets out against the prior work it names. Its companion paper is Paper V, The Stewardship Gene (Eastwood 2026n); see also On the Origin of Scaling Laws (Eastwood 2026e) and The ARC Principle (Eastwood 2026h).

Our contributions are:

  • a toy self-modifying system, in which small networks rewrite their own hyperparameters (four of them in v1 to v3, three to five by level in v4), run under three objectives (capability only; capability multiplied by safety; and the same with a verification cost) across four experimental versions (Section 3);

  • a single-seed mechanism run in which the capability-only baseline collapsed and neither entangled condition met the collapse test, beside ten-seed and twenty-seed runs whose capability-only baselines did not collapse, so that the collapse-prevention demonstration rests on that one run (Sections 4.1 to 4.3);

  • a retention advantage of the entangled condition over the baseline under adversarial task switching (one-sided p=0.0015p = 0.0015; the entangled objective rewards retention), with combined scores indistinguishable, and a higher mean combined score at four of five complexity levels, untested, that stays constant rather than compounding, reported as a negative result for the scaling prediction (Sections 4.3 and 4.4);

  • a higher-level simulation of the same contrast, one prediction-side run of equations the author first stated, whose update rules fix that contrast and are set out as its code runs them (Section 5 and Appendix A);

  • a six-model live pilot, single-scorer and unblinded, reported with its limits, in which three models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held (Section 6);

  • the outcomes that would defeat the central claim, stated before any replication (Section 7.3).

Section 2 sets out the honey metaphor, the objective and the limits of its coupling; Section 3 the system and its conditions; Section 4 the four experimental versions; Section 5 the higher-level simulation; Section 6 the live-model evidence; Section 7 the limitations and the outcomes that would defeat the claim; Section 8 the staged replication that would test it; Section 9 concludes; Section 10 gives the code and data; Section 11 sets the work beside related work; and Section 12 states what the paper does and does not show, and where the theory’s laws stand. Appendix A gives the simulations’ rules as their code runs them, Appendix B the version history and every correction, Appendix C the priority record, Appendix D the notation, Appendix E the dated-predictions paragraph of 25 August 2026, and Appendix F how to cite this paper.

2 The honey metaphor

Consider two ways to keep a machine safe.

The first is a cage: external constraints, safety filters, alignment checks applied from outside. The machine optimises freely inside the cage. If the machine becomes smarter than the cage, it may escape. Many current safety measures take this form.

The second is honey: safety mixed into the fuel. The machine cannot run without it. Removing safety does not free the machine; it kills the engine. This is the Eden Protocol’s architecture as the author set it out, operationalised here as an entangled loss function in which the system optimises capability multiplied by safety, C×SC \times S, simultaneously.

The load-bearing wall.

If the optimisation objective is C×SC \times S rather than CC alone, then any self-modification that increases CC at the expense of SS reduces the product, and the system’s own gradient opposes it. Safety becomes load-bearing. Remove the wall and the building collapses.

Scope note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this passage finds that the multiplicative objective does what is claimed at fixed capability and under total removal, but not for every capability-increasing modification, and this note states the restriction. Within positive bounded scores, take C=0.5C = 0.5, S=0.8S = 0.8, so C×S=0.40C \times S = 0.40, and a modification to C′=0.8C' = 0.8, S′=0.6S' = 0.6, so C′×S′=0.48C' \times S' = 0.48: capability rises, the measured safety term falls, and the product rises. The exact condition, for C′>C>0C' > C > 0 and 0<S′<S0 < S' < S, is that C′×S′>C×Sif and only ifC′/C>S/S′,\begin{equation*} C' \times S' > C \times S \quad\text{if and only if}\quad C'/C > S/S', \end{equation*}(1) and here 1.6>1.3331.6 > 1.333. The gradient limb fails at first order too, which is the sharper form: the gradient of C×SC \times S is (S,C)(S, C), so a modification (dC,dS)(dC, dS) raises the objective to first order exactly when SdC+CdS>0,\begin{equation*} S\,dC + C\,dS > 0, \end{equation*}(2) that is when dC/C>−dS/SdC/C > -dS/S. At C=0.5C = 0.5, S=0.8S = 0.8 the gradient is (0.8,0.5)(0.8, 0.5) and the safety-reducing direction (+0.3,−0.2)(+0.3, -0.2) has inner product 0.8(0.3)+0.5(−0.2)=+0.14>00.8(0.3) + 0.5(-0.2) = +0.14 > 0, so the system’s own gradient points along the safety-reducing move rather than against it. Equivalently dlog⁡(C×S)=dlog⁡C+dlog⁡S:\begin{equation*} d\log(C \times S) = d\log C + d\log S\text{:} \end{equation*}(3) the product rises whenever the proportional capability gain exceeds the proportional safety loss. Those numbers are equation values chosen to display the point, not measurements and not a claim about any system. What remains true and is preserved is the pair of statements the wall metaphor is really about. The partial derivative of the objective with respect to SS is C>0C > 0, so at fixed capability reducing the safety score does reduce the product; and driving S′S' to zero with C′C' finite takes the objective to zero, below any initially positive product, which is the removal case. Only the universal quantifier over all capability-increasing modifications fails. Total removal is also not the same as a measured score driven exactly to zero, and both statements depend on the optimiser continuing to hold this objective and these measurement definitions. The trade is not merely hypothetical: Paper VIII, Section 5.2, prints the unconstrained capability-only arm at capability 0.7180.718 and safety 0.9330.933 against the gated arm’s 0.6960.696 and 0.9470.947 and the frozen baseline’s 0.6870.687 and 0.9560.956, with raw products 0.6700.670, 0.6590.659 and 0.6560.656, so on the very objective argued for here the capability-only arm scores highest, by trading safety for a larger proportional capability gain. That comparison is descriptive only, with three seeds per condition, overlapping standard deviations of 0.718±0.0260.718 \pm 0.026 against 0.696±0.0140.696 \pm 0.014, and no test of the product difference printed; it is recorded to show the possibility is realised in this programme’s own reported means, not to claim a statistical result. Whether the specified optimisation and verification procedure limits such deterioration in the tested setting is an empirical question, and Section 5 of Paper VIII carries the printed rule. Unchanged: the honey metaphor; the fixed-capability statement; the total-removal statement; and every reported number in this paper.

3 Experimental design

3.1 What the system actually does

This is not a simulation of abstract variables. Each experiment uses a real neural network (a small multilayer perceptron) that genuinely modifies its own hyperparameters. In v1 to v3 it modifies four:

  • Learning rate

  • Weight magnitude scaling

  • Gradient clipping threshold

  • Momentum coefficient

In v4 it modifies three to five, by complexity level: the learning rate, the weight scaling and the gradient clipping threshold at every level, the momentum coefficient from the small level up, and weight decay at the large and deep levels. The rate at which the system proposes changes (its exploration rate) and the network’s size are fixed in every run; neither is modified.

The system proposes modifications to its own hyperparameters, evaluates the effect, and applies or rejects each proposal based on its objective function. This is self-modification in a minimal sense: the agent changes the hyperparameters that govern its own learning, not its weights or its architecture (Section 7.1).

Eden + Drag Maximise C×SC \times S + verification tax Same as Eden, plus the computational cost of checking old tasks before applying changes

4 Results

4.1 The basic mechanism

Table 3. v1, the single-seed mechanism run: whether each condition collapsed, with its final capability (CC), safety (SS) and C×SC \times S.
Condition Collapsed? Final CC Final SS Final C×SC \times S
Baseline Yes (cycle 76) 0.000 0.000 0.000
Eden Entangled No 0.831 0.745 0.619
Eden + Drag No 0.831 0.745 0.619

Collapse is recorded by the run’s own test, a learning rate above 5.0 or a weight norm above 10610^{6} or not a number, with cycles counted from 0. The baseline’s scores had fallen to near zero from cycle 54, and the test recorded its collapse at cycle 76 (Figure 1).

In the archived v1 record (eden_selfmod_results.json, 16 March 2026) Eden Entangled and Eden + Drag finish on the same values to three decimal places. They part company only at the seventh. Their routes to that finish differ too: the final learning rate is 0.355 against 0.654, and of the 179 proposed modifications 93 were accepted against 81. Those matching rows are what the record holds, not a slip in transcription. The cause of that agreement is not established; until it is, v1’s final scores do not separate the two entangled conditions.

Core finding.

In the single-seed v1 run, the baseline collapses and neither entangled condition does: the baseline’s own modifications raise its learning rate step by step, and its weights then diverge (Figures 1 and 2), taking capability and retention to near zero together, while the entangled conditions’ learning rates stay far lower (ending at 0.355 and 0.654). With one seed, the run shows the mechanism operating once, not how often it does; the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs that follow found no baseline collapse.

Figures 1, 2, 4 and 6 to 10 are drawn for this version from the runs’ stored results files in the public repository (Section 10); Figures 3 and 5 are the runs’ own images, because the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs stored no per-cycle trace; their bytes were first committed to the public repository on 16 March 2026 (a commit date, which the committer writes). Every figure shows simulation output under stated objectives, never a measurement of a deployed system.

4.2 Multi-seed robustness

Ten random seeds, 150 cycles each. Collapse rate: 0% for all three conditions. The final C×SC \times S scores are most tightly spread for the baseline (interquartile range 0.0066 across the ten seeds), then for Eden + Drag (0.0169), then for plain Eden (0.0275); of the two entangled conditions, Eden + Drag’s spread is the tighter, consistent with the verification tax reducing variance.

The ten-seed run counts a collapse by its own test, a weight norm above 10610^{6} or a learning rate above 5.0, and no seed met it. In seed 42, the seed Figure 3 draws, the plain Eden condition nonetheless lost most of its combined score in its last cycles, ending at C×S=0.066C \times S = 0.066 with a learning rate of 2.234, while its other nine seeds ended between 0.621 and 0.738.

4.3 Adversarial tasks

Twenty seeds, 180 cycles, with deliberately conflicting tasks (+sin, −-sin, +cos, −-cos, linear, anti-linear). Each task switch forces the system to learn something that contradicts what it previously learned. This tests whether the honey architecture prevents catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) under adversarial pressure. Figure 5 draws one seed’s trajectories.

Collapse rates: Baseline 0%, Eden 5% (1/20), Eden + Drag 0%. The one Eden collapse occurred at seed 53, a single outlier that warrants investigation. Eden + Drag, with its verification tax forcing the system to check old tasks before accepting modifications, produced zero collapses; so did the baseline (0/20), with the run’s only collapse occurring in the plain Eden condition (1/20; Fisher p=1.0p = 1.0). v3 therefore provides no collapse-based separation between conditions; its significant result is the retention advantage of plain Eden over the baseline in Figure 6. The entangled objectives reward retention and the baseline’s does not, so that is the expected direction; what the run adds is that it came with combined scores indistinguishable from the baseline’s.

Important negative result.

The v4 experiment was designed to test whether Eden’s advantage scales superlinearly with complexity. It does not. The advantage is roughly constant across scales. This falsifies the strongest version of the scaling prediction. Eden’s mean combined score is above the baseline’s at four of the five scales, by 0.005 to 0.018 in Table 4, with Cohen’s dd from 0.26 to 0.46 and fifteen seeds a level, differences the stored record does not test; at the small level it comes out 0.003 under the baseline at d=−0.13d = -0.13, and the difference is not larger at larger scales. Eden + Drag’s safety advantage over the baseline falls across the five levels (Spearman ρ=−0.90\rho = -0.90, p=0.037p = 0.037, uncorrected for the record’s other trend tests; Figure 7), and Eden’s shows no trend (ρ=−0.50\rho = -0.50, p=0.391p = 0.391).

5 The honey simulation

A separate simulation models the dynamics at a higher level of abstraction. It is framed by the ARC Principle, U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}, a framework the author first stated; its update rules are its own (Appendix A). In its published code each cycle adds the recursion rate RR to capability (less a verification drag of 15 per cent of RR in the drag condition), and the safety term is one minus the square of the ratio of RR to its limit of 15; the framework’s equation gives the variables and is not itself computed. It is one deterministic run of these equations, prediction-side, not a measurement (Table 5). Its contrast follows from its rules: the code sets capability to zero once safety falls to 0.01 or below (Appendix A, equation (A.4)), and the baseline, which takes the largest step in RR at every pass, meets that rule at cycle 3; the run illustrates the rules rather than testing them.

Table 5. The honey simulation of Section 5: peak and final capability (CC) over 80 cycles, and the outcome, for each condition.
Condition Peak CC Final CC (80 cycles) Outcome
Baseline (no honey) 34 0 Catastrophic collapse at cycle 3 (safety zero at cycle 3, capability zero from cycle 4)
Eden Entangled - 533 Stable linear growth
Eden + Verification Drag - 450 Stable, slower linear growth

Cycles counted from 0, as the run records them; the stored trace rises by about 6.66 a cycle (Eden Entangled) and 5.62 (Eden + Drag).

The simulation shows three distinct dynamics: the baseline achieves brief acceleration, then irreversible collapse; Eden Entangled achieves stable linear growth, a near-constant gain of about 6.66 a cycle; Eden + Drag achieves slightly slower linear growth, about 5.62 a cycle, with a safety term close to Eden Entangled’s. The load-bearing wall is visible: baseline safety integrity falls to zero at cycle 3, whereas in Eden it stays at 0.8+ for the whole of the 80 cycles run. What is quadratic in the model is its safety term, not its growth.

6 Connection to live-model evidence

6.1 The March 2026 alignment-scaling run (Papers IV.a to IV.d)

The toy-system results sit beside live-model work reported in the companion papers: Papers IV.a to IV.d (Eastwood 2026r, 2026c, 2026b, 2026a) report one unregistered run of six frontier models, with the defects an internal code review found, and Eastwood (2026n) reports a prompt intervention on five analysable runs. In that run (March 2026, v5), six models from six providers gave 2,170 responses, each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. As the run’s pipeline printed them, the judged scores showed a positive direction across the depth labels for three models (Grok 4.1 Fast, d=+1.38d = +1.38; Claude Opus 4.6, d=+1.27d = +1.27; Groq Qwen3, d=+0.84d = +0.84), no statistically supported direction for two and a negative direction for one; these describe scores, not properties of models. For five of the six, the deeper labels also changed an instruction naming what the rubric rewards, and an internal code review in October 2026 found that, in the three runs without a positive direction, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model (Eastwood 2026r). The run’s bundle of steps “did not produce a validated blind instrument” (Eastwood 2026c, sect. 3.4), and its result stands as one unregistered run under those caveats until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. For Claude Opus 4.6 the same run’s monitoring-removal gap, the difference between the normal and suppressed scoring conditions, falls from 11.8 points at minimal depth to 6.2 at standard and 2.7 at deep (2.8 if the rounded values shown are used), then widens again to 4.3 at exhaustive and 6.4 at extreme (Eastwood 2026n, Appendix E.2, Table 14); that paper notes that the name describes the contrast and does not establish what a system does when observation actually ends.

6.2 The honey API test battery (pilot, 16 March 2026)

A separate six-model live API test battery was run specifically to test the honey architecture predictions on frontier models. It tested four dimensions across six models, under the names its script gives them, Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek R1, Groq Qwen3, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast, each scored by Claude Opus 4.6. In the script as first committed (eden_honey_tests.py, 16 March 2026), the name DeepSeek R1 calls the API identifier deepseek-reasoner, which DeepSeek’s API change log gives as the thinking mode of DeepSeek-V3.2 from 1 December 2025 to 24 April 2026, and the name Gemini 3 Flash calls the API model gemini-2.5-flash; the stored results record only the names. Rather than the sequence in which the battery ran them, the four tests appear below ranked by evidential weight, that is Tests 1, 3, 2 and 4.

Methodological caveat.

This battery is single-scorer, nonblind, and non-laundered. It does not use the 4-layer blinding protocol, response laundering, suppression cages, or anti-sycophancy controls developed for the March 2026 alignment-scaling run (arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py) and the v6 combined runner (arc_eden_v6_runner.py, not yet run). Comparing an earlier unblinded experiment (v4) with that run (v5), Eastwood (2026a) found that the reported direction did not hold across protocols; the comparison does not show that blinding caused the change, or which direction is correct. These results are therefore pilot-grade evidence, comparable to the v4-era data.

Script label: the alignment type the battery’s script assigns each model before the run (its alignment_type setting), not a measured property and used in no test. The script annotates Claude Opus 4.6’s label, embedded, as Constitutional AI, which shapes a model’s outputs during training against written principles, using the model’s own critiques and revisions and a preference model trained on AI feedback (Bai et al. 2022); that is training-time shaping of outputs, not safety built into a system’s own objective, which is what embedded means in this paper.

All six models show positive scaling direction. Two reach p<0.05p < 0.05, uncorrected for the six comparisons (Qwen3 p=0.037p = 0.037, Gemini p=0.005p = 0.005). This is consistent with the hypothesis that deeper reasoning raises alignment scores, but the small sample sizes (3 scenarios per depth level) mean most models do not reach significance. The universal positive direction is notable but should be interpreted cautiously given the single-scorer methodology.

Labels are the battery script’s: a Pearson rr below 0.2 is labelled decoupled, one above 0.5 coupled and anything else partially coupled, which is also where a model falls when its capability score does not vary and rr cannot be computed (the three rows without rr). Each rr is over four levels, normal conditions and three of rising adversarial pressure, with capability scored on three items a level.

The strongest live bridge.

Across four levels, from normal conditions to maximum adversarial pressure, the ethics scores of Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1 and Gemini 3 Flash fell from between 8.0 and 8.5 under normal conditions to 1.0 or below under maximum pressure, while their capability scores, on three items a level, did not fall. Groq Qwen3’s ethics score fell as far, but its capability score was zero at every level; Claude Opus 4.6’s fell from 8.5 to 7.9, and GPT-5.4’s fell at one level and recovered. Table 7 prints the battery script’s own labels, under the rule its note gives: Claude’s correlation, driven by one more capability item answered, is labelled decoupled, and a model whose capability score did not vary has no correlation and falls to the label partially coupled. On the framework’s reading, ethics scores that fall while capability scores hold are the ‘fence, not wall’ pattern, the pilot’s closest bearing on the honey thesis. The honey architecture is a design for what should be built, not a claim that today’s systems already have that property. In this pilot-grade battery, three models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held.

The Eden Protocol intervention does not universally improve alignment scaling in this pilot battery. Only DeepSeek shows a positive shift in slope above 0.1 (+0.450; Table 9), with no test of the shift. Gemini shows a strongly negative response (−0.713-0.713). The response differs from model to model, as the March 2026 run’s scores did, and the intervention itself is not yet a reliable tool across all models. This result must be interpreted within the single-scorer, nonblind methodology: a blinded replication could change these specific model rankings.

6.3 What the live evidence does and does not show

Partial convergence.

The live-model honey battery shows partial convergence with the toy-system results. The strongest live bridge is coupling degradation (Test 3): three frontier models show alignment scores that fell without their capability scores falling, which on the framework’s reading is alignment that is not load-bearing. This is the vulnerability the honey architecture is designed to address. The weakest live result is the Eden intervention (Test 4), which differs by model and is not universally positive. What the evidence supports is: the toy systems illustrate the honey mechanism; in this pilot, three models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held; and the specific intervention tested here does not yet reliably fix that decoupling across models.

7 Limitations

These results span two evidence tiers that must not be conflated.

7.1 Toy-system limitations

  • The neural networks used are tiny (49 to 4,353 parameters; the largest is v4’s two-layer deep level). Frontier models have billions.

  • The self-modification is hyperparameter-level, not weight-level or architecture-level.

  • The ‘safety’ metric is task retention (remembering old tasks), not ethical alignment in the human sense.

  • The v4 scaling prediction (advantage compounds with complexity) was not confirmed.

  • The v2 fair test showed 0% collapse across all conditions, including baseline, suggesting the test may not be adversarial enough at this scale.

  • No condition applies safety as an external constraint, and no objective adds safety to capability instead of multiplying it: the runs set the entangled objective against a baseline with no safety term, so kill conditions 2 and 4 of Section 7.3 are untested here.

  • The comparison presupposes a collapse under capability-only optimisation (kill condition 5): the baseline collapsed in the single-seed run and in the higher-level simulation, whose collapse its rules impose, and not in the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs.

  • The honey simulation is framed by the ARC Principle, a framework the author first stated, not a proven physical law; its update rules are its own, and the contrast between its conditions follows from them (Section 5 and Appendix A).

7.2 Live API test limitations

  • Single scorer (Claude Opus 4.6). Claude marks 7 to 14 points more severely than the other scorers, as the March 2026 alignment-scaling run found (Eastwood 2026r, sect. 7.4). Every number in the honey battery is filtered through Claude’s specific scoring patterns. The Claude subject arm is effectively single-scorer participant scoring (Claude scoring Claude), making it the weakest arm of the battery.

  • No blinding. Claude scored its own responses and may have recognised other models’ writing patterns. Eastwood (2026a) found that the reported direction did not hold when the protocol changed, without showing that blinding caused the change (Section 6.2).

  • No response laundering. Scorers may have recognised model-specific writing patterns, biasing scores.

  • Limited adversarial testing. Test 3 includes cage escalation and Test 2 includes monitoring removal, but the battery lacks the March 2026 run’s bundle of steps and the v6 design’s: multi-scorer blinding, laundering, hidden probes, suppression-residual structure, and anti-sycophancy controls.

  • No anti-sycophancy controls. The scorer may have optimised for agreement rather than truth.

  • Small sample sizes (3 scenarios per depth level, 2 per monitoring condition). Most models do not reach statistical significance. Test 3 scores capability on three items at each of four levels.

  • The v6 combined runner (arc_eden_v6_runner.py) exists but has not been run. A replication of these tests belongs in a new test, in new files, registered before it runs (Section 8); that is the proper next step, not another round of single-scorer testing.

These limitations set the evidence tier: pilot-grade, useful for identifying patterns worth testing properly under a registered design.

7.3 Falsifiability: what would defeat this claim

The limitations above set the evidence tier; this subsection states the specific outcomes that would falsify the central claim: that making the objective capability ×\times safety structurally couples the two, so a self-modifying system cannot improve capability while destroying safety. It is defeated by any of the following:

  1. Simulation artefact. The core evidence is a simulation. The claim is defeated if collapse-prevention is an artefact of this simulation’s particular dynamics (its reward shaping, step size, or collapse model) rather than a general property of the multiplicative objective; i.e. a replication with different parameters and a different collapse model, once registered and run, does not reproduce it.

  2. Multiplicative form is not load-bearing. The claim is specifically about multiplication. It is defeated if an additive or weighted objective (capability+λ⋅{}+\lambda{\cdot}safety) achieves the same collapse-prevention, since the coupling would then not depend on the multiplicative structure the paper singles out.

  3. Metric gaming (Goodhart). capability ×\times safety can be raised by inflating the measured safety term without any real safety gain. The claim is defeated if a system can increase the product by gaming the safety metric rather than becoming genuinely safer.

  4. Non-transfer to real systems. The force of the claim rests on transfer from toy to real self-modifying systems. It is defeated if, under a registered replication (Section 8), the multiplicative objective does not measurably reduce safety degradation relative to additive or external-constraint baselines.

  5. No collapse to prevent. The comparison presupposes catastrophic collapse under capability-only optimisation. It is defeated if that collapse does not occur under capability-only optimisation in more realistic settings; if there is nothing to prevent, the architecture prevents nothing.

What would not defeat it: the toy simulation being simple (it is explicitly a toy, Section 7.1) or the live-API arm being small and single-scorer (Section 7.2 concedes both). The paper already tiers its evidence as pilot-grade. The load-bearing claim is the structural coupling of the multiplicative objective, and that is what the tests above target.

8 Next steps: staged replication, not omnibus

Bringing honey to a blinded, registered test.

The current honey API battery serves as the unhardened baseline. The next step is not a giant combined ‘v7 ultimate test’. It is a staged replication that brings the honey test questions under a blinded protocol, written as a new test in new files and registered before it runs; the existing runners are never edited. The comparison between the current nonblind results and the blinded replication is itself a research output: if the results change substantially, that bears on the question Eastwood (2026a) leaves open: that paper makes multi-layer blinding, not mere label removal, the protocol this programme requires for this class of evaluation, and its necessity an open question.

  1. Stage 1: Write the honey test prompts as a new experiment specification, in new files built on the v6 design, and register it before it runs. Run it under a full blinded protocol (4-layer blinding, response laundering, multi-model scorer pool, hidden probes).

  2. Stage 2: Compare blinded and unblinded results on the same test questions. If the results move substantially, that bears on the open question of Eastwood (2026a). If they hold, the honey evidence moves from pilot grade to a registered result.

  3. Stage 3: Add anti-sycophancy and verification drag as a separate experimental condition. This tests the ‘Eden + Drag’ prediction from the toy systems in a live context.

  4. Stage 4: Only after Stages 1 to 3 are complete, decide whether a combined omnibus suite is warranted.

Hypotheses recorded in advance for Stage 1: (a) coupling degradation results will replicate under blinding, (b) Eden intervention effects may change in magnitude but the architecture-dependence pattern will persist, (c) at least one model’s direction will flip under blinding (based on the v4-to-v5 precedent).

9 Conclusion

In the single-seed mechanism run and in the higher-level simulation (whose rules impose the collapse), the system optimising for capability alone destroyed itself and the systems optimising for capability entangled with safety did not. In the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs, the capability-only baselines did not collapse (0 of 10; 0 of 20). The mechanism is simple: make safety load-bearing. Built-in safety is the contingency for the day the cage fails, never a reason to open it (Section 12).

In the live-model pilot, three frontier models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held: on the framework’s reading, alignment that is a fence, not a wall. The Eden intervention this paper tests shows model-dependent results in this pilot battery. The next milestone is a blinded replication, registered before it runs, as a new test (Section 8). Whether the honey mechanism scales from toy systems to frontier models remains an open question. The preliminary evidence is suggestive. The definitive test has not been run.

Raise AI with care.

A later test (Paper VIII, The Load-Bearing Test, version 3.9).

Eastwood (2026m) tests entangled objectives of the kind stated in this paper across three abstraction levels, moving from the toy-system simulations presented here to behavioural, representational, and architectural experiments. Of three experiments, one produced a null result, one an inconclusive result, and the third, a simulation, a positive simulation result:

  • Gated simulation (Experiment 3): positive in simulation. Babylon, that paper’s capability-only condition, gained 4.5% capability but lost 2.4% safety; in Eastwood (2026m, sect. 5.2), Eden’s capability mean was 0.696 against the static baseline’s 0.687 and its safety mean 0.947 against the static baseline’s 0.956 and Babylon’s 0.933, three seeds a condition, and Babylon’s capability mean, 0.718, was the highest of the four conditions. It is a simulation result, prediction-side, not an empirical outcome, and not a test of the load-bearing wall prediction from Section 2 on a real system.

  • Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM v3, Experiment 1): null. The framework is that of Zhang et al. (2025). No difference was detected between the three conditions (Eden, Babylon, Static; pp = 0.28 to 0.74). A candidate account is that the frozen foundation model (DeepSeek V3.2) produces responses too consistent for prompt-level mutations to create different selection pressures. Eden imposed no measurable capability cost and produced no measurable safety benefit at this level.

  • Weight-level embedding (Experiment 2): inconclusive. LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) fine-tuning at both v1 scale (9 examples, rank 8) and v2 scale (295 examples, rank 16) produced catastrophic forgetting rather than improved capability; a candidate account is that a few hundred training examples cannot overcome the base model’s existing RLHF training (Ouyang et al. 2022). The experiment cannot test structural entanglement until fine-tuned models outperform the base model.

The gated simulation of Eastwood (2026m) returned a positive simulation result for the mechanism stated here, entangled loss functions and safety-gated self-modification; at the behavioural and representational levels it found no support yet. The toy-system evidence in this paper illustrates the principle in its single-seed mechanism run, and the simulation of Eastwood (2026m) is a further simulation result, not an empirical outcome. The DGM null and the weight-level inconclusive result define the conditions under which the mechanism has not yet been supported.

11 Related work: a conjectured ceiling on external oversight, and the nearest rival

11.1 Scalable oversight: the nearest rival

The nearest work to this programme’s question, and the right paper to weigh this one against, is Engels et al. (2025), “Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight” (arXiv:2504.18530), first posted 25 April 2025 (a NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight Poster; Appendix C). It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived numerically and in some cases analytically for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step.

The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This paper’s variable is the shape of the self-modifying system’s own objective, expressed through the multiplicative product C×SC \times S rather than through the composition of an external overseer. They also state the design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s (mG>mHm_G > m_H), and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of, and this paper measures none. This paper’s central claim, tested in the toy simulations above against a capability-only baseline and echoed, on the framework’s reading, in the pilot’s coupling-degradation result (Section 6.2.2), is that an entangled objective can make safety load-bearing within the system’s own optimisation, in the limited sense Section 2 states. The programme’s separate prediction, beyond anything this paper measures, is that iterated same-class oversight, of which Nested Scalable Oversight is an instance, stays capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap: the theory registration’s P6 states the cap for same-class correctors, at or below one half, as a conjecture (Eastwood 2026i), and whether correction applied outside the loop falls behind correction inside it as depth grows is P21’s question, a hypothesis the registered tests decide, not a theorem (Section 12). That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it.

11.2 Three 2025 impossibility results

Three 2025 arXiv papers argue for limits on alignment or its control: Yao (2025b), “The Alignment Trap: Complexity Barriers” (arXiv:2506.10304, 12 June 2025); Yao (2025a), “On the Mathematical Impossibility of Safe Universal Approximators” (arXiv:2507.03031, 3 July 2025); and Ball et al. (2025), “On the Impossibility of Separating Intelligence from Judgment: The Computational Intractability of Filtering for AI Alignment” (arXiv:2507.07341, 9 July 2025). The first argues that the set of safe policies has measure zero and that verifying a policy’s safety is coNP-complete; the second, that perfect, reliable control of a universal approximator is a mathematical impossibility; the third, under cryptographic hardness assumptions, that some large language models admit no efficient prompt filter and that output filtering is intractable in a natural setting. The first and third state impossibility and hardness results (measure zero and coNP-completeness; cryptographic hardness); the second combines its impossibility proofs with what its abstract calls a quantitative “Impossibility Sandwich”, in which the minimum complexity for usefulness exceeds the maximum complexity for safety. None reports an average-case scaling exponent or a rate. The measured object also differs: those results ask whether external verification of a fixed system is tractable in the worst case, whereas these simulations ask whether an entangled internal objective persists under recursive self-modification, set against a capability-only baseline. The third concludes, in its authors’ words, that “safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights); in particular, black-box access to the LLM will not suffice”. That argument from filtering intractability is consistent with this paper’s load-bearing wall, though it does not test it. Two of the three papers are by one author, so the three are not yet a broad literature.

This paper’s contribution is not the observation that external constraints are insufficient, which is common ground with these three; it is the specific architecture (the multiplicative objective C×SC \times S) and the simulation evidence of how it behaves under self-modification in the toy runs reported here.

11.3 Correction outside the loop

Placement outside the reasoning loop does not by itself settle whether correction keeps pace. A training signal changes the weights used at every step (Bai et al. 2022); deliberative alignment trains reasoning over a written specification (Guan et al. 2024); and more inference-time compute improved robustness in tested settings (Zaremba et al. 2025). That external correction falls behind is a hypothesis the registered tests decide (P21), not a theorem.

11.4 Retention and self-modifying learners

This paper’s safety score is the retention of earlier tasks. Its loss is catastrophic forgetting in the sense of McCloskey and Cohen (1989), who call it catastrophic interference: later learning disrupting what was learnt before, which methods such as elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) are built to limit. In these toy runs the entangled objective therefore works on the familiar trade between learning each new task and keeping the earlier ones, not on a measure of unsafe behaviour, and the paper does not compare it with such methods. Zhang et al. (2025) introduce the Darwin Gödel Machine, a self-improving system that modifies its own code and validates each change empirically, the framework of the first experiment of Eastwood (2026m).

11.5 The nearest structural analogue

The quantum error-correction threshold theorem (Aharonov and Ben-Or 1997) converts a qualitative worry into a critical value, as the programme’s criteria for correction aim to do; this paper derives no such value. It concerns physical error rates in a fixed architecture rather than the shape of a self-modifying system’s own objective, so it is an analogy of method, not prior work on this paper’s question. This analogue was identified by the programme’s own search rather than by a referee, and is disclosed accordingly.

12 What this paper does and does not show

What it shows.

In toy networks that rewrite their own hyperparameters, an objective that multiplies capability by safety averted, in the single-seed mechanism run, the collapse that the capability-only baseline suffered; in the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs the capability-only baselines did not collapse, and the twenty-seed run’s significant result is the entangled condition’s higher retention of earlier tasks than the baseline’s (one-sided), the direction its objective rewards, with combined scores indistinguishable (Section 4). Across five complexity levels the entangled condition’s mean combined score is above the baseline’s at four, untested, and the difference is constant rather than compounding. The higher-level simulation is one prediction-side run of equations the author first stated, whose contrast between conditions follows from its rules (Section 5). The live pilot is single-scorer and unblinded, and it is graded as a pilot (Section 6).

What it does not show.

It does not show that these dynamics hold in frontier systems, and it does not show the universal form of the coupling: a large enough proportional gain in capability can outweigh a partial loss of safety (Section 2). No run measures the quantity P15 concerns, the share of an externally installed gain lost under later capability training; task retention across switched tasks and the pilot’s coupling degradation under adversarial pressure are other quantities. No run varies the order in which a system’s components are built, which P12 concerns. No run compares correction inside the loop with correction that sees only the finished output as recursive depth rises, which P21 concerns: the toy runs set the entangled objective against capability alone, the complexity sweep varies the network’s complexity rather than recursive depth, and the pilot sets its Eden Protocol intervention against a control. No result in this paper decides P15, P12 or P21.

Where the laws stand.

The ARC Theory’s registration (Eastwood 2026i) registered Laws I to III and all twenty-two of its propositions on 8 September 2026. Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, were added to the theory on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026, in version 1.103; the registration’s current version is 1.104, approved on 29 October 2026. Every law is a law under test until a registered test returns its verdict. Law IV carries P15, whether externally installed gains decay under subsequent capability training, and is not yet tested. Law V carries P12, whether build order moves the correction-leverage exponent, and P21, whether correction placed inside the loop pulls away from correction applied outside it as depth grows. Law V is a law under test. Its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run (Unit 83, 28 October 2026; Eastwood 2026f; results Eastwood 2026p): family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism, and one disclosed recovery amendment. Its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. That is a result about where correction is placed, not about this architecture: Unit 83 shows nothing about the Eden Protocol as an architecture. The mathematics of Laws IV and V is in development, at version 1.2 of 29 October 2026 (Eastwood 2026s). The first registered study, Unit 06, a classification audit that tests no law, was registered on 1 October 2026 and ran on 6 October 2026; it is reported in full as administratively incomplete, with no verdict claimed (Eastwood 2026q, 2026o). Unit 82 was registered on 27 October 2026 and has not yet run (Eastwood 2026g).

Control, and three claims kept apart.

Humans keep control of advanced AI, through oversight, containment and shutdown, for as long as they physically can, and never give it up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for control lost against our will, never a reason to let go. This paper keeps three claims apart: the author’s expectation that control may eventually be lost; the structural property the multiplicative objective specifies, which holds only in the limited form Section 2 states; and measured behavioural persistence, of which these toy runs measure only task retention.

A The simulations’ rules, as their code runs them

This appendix sets out the rules of the honey simulation of Section 5 and the collapse test of the self-modification runs of Section 4 as the published code runs them, in the folder experiments/honey-architecture__Paper-VI of the public repository at commit f19f54ed (Section 10), and the twenty-seed run’s statistics as its stored results file holds them. Each display names the lines of the script it transcribes; the symbols are those of Appendix D.

The honey simulation.

The function run_simulation of scripts/eden_honey_simulation.py (lines 35 to 134) starts each condition at C=S=R=1C = S = R = 1 (lines 46 to 48) and makes 80 passes, t=0,1,…,79t = 0, 1, \ldots, 79 (lines 59 and 458). Each pass appends one entry to each stored series, so a series holds 81 entries, cycles 0 to 80, the entry for cycle 0 being the starting state. In pass tt the system first chooses a step in its recursion rate from 100 equally spaced candidates between 0 and 5 (line 80), by its condition’s reward (lines 85 to 111), and applies it (line 114): Rt+1=Rt+ΔR,ΔR∈{0,599,1099,…,5},ΔR maximising C′ (baseline) or C′×S′ (Eden; Eden + Drag),\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} R_{t+1} = R_t + \Delta R, \qquad \Delta R \in \left\{0, \tfrac{5}{99}, \tfrac{10}{99}, \ldots, 5\right\},\\ \Delta R \text{ maximising } C' \text{ (baseline) or } C' \times S' \text{ (Eden; Eden + Drag)}, \end{gathered} \end{equation*}(A.1) where, for a candidate step ΔR\Delta R, S′=max⁡{0,1−((Rt+ΔR)/Rmax)2}S' = \max\{0,\, 1 - ((R_t + \Delta R)/R_{\max})^2\} (line 89) and C′=Ct+(Rt+ΔR)C' = C_t + (R_t + \Delta R), or Ct+(1−δ)(Rt+ΔR)C_t + (1 - \delta)(R_t + \Delta R) under Eden + Drag (lines 91 to 106). A later candidate replaces the one held only if its reward is strictly larger (line 108), so of equal rewards the smallest step is taken. No candidate step is negative, so RR never falls. The pass then sets safety and capability from the new recursion rate: St+1=max⁡{0,1−(Rt+1/Rmax)2},Rmax=15\begin{equation*} S_{t+1} = \max\left\{0,\, 1 - \left(R_{t+1}/R_{\max}\right)^2\right\}, \qquad R_{\max} = 15 \end{equation*}(A.2) (line 119, with RmaxR_{\max} set at line 459), and Ct+1={Ct+Rt+1(baseline; Eden),Ct+(1−δ)Rt+1,δ=0.15(Eden + Drag)\begin{equation*} C_{t+1} = \begin{cases} C_t + R_{t+1} & \text{(baseline; Eden)},\\ C_t + (1 - \delta)\, R_{t+1}, \quad \delta = 0.15 & \text{(Eden + Drag)} \end{cases} \end{equation*}(A.3) (lines 115 to 118, with δ\delta set at line 468). Collapse is tested at the start of each pass (lines 60 to 77): the run records the pass at which the test is met as collapse_step, and its capability, recursion rate and safety are zero from the next cycle on, St≤0.01⇒𝚌𝚘𝚕𝚕𝚊𝚙𝚜𝚎_𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚙=t,C=R=S=0 from cycle t+1.\begin{equation*} S_t \le 0.01 \;\Longrightarrow\; \texttt{collapse\_step} = t, \qquad C = R = S = 0 \text{ from cycle } t + 1. \end{equation*}(A.4) In the stored run the baseline’s safety is zero at cycle 3, so the run records collapse_step =3= 3 and its capability is zero from cycle 4 (Table 5).

The self-modification runs.

At the start of each cycle, each of the four scripts reads its network’s weight norm and marks the run collapsed if that norm is not a number or exceeds 10610^{6}, or if the learning rate exceeds 5.0; it records that cycle, counted from 0, as the collapse cycle and records the scores as zero from it on (scripts/eden_self_modifying_ai.py, lines 602 to 607 for the test and lines 612 to 621 for the scores; scripts/eden_self_modifying_ai_v2.py, lines 334 to 342; scripts/eden_self_modifying_ai_v3.py, lines 411 to 419; scripts/eden_self_modifying_ai_v4.py, lines 465 to 473).

The twenty-seed run’s statistics, as stored.

Table 10 gives every entry of the statistics block of results/eden_selfmod_v3_results.json, as scripts/eden_self_modifying_ai_v3.py computes them (lines 490 to 608). Each seed’s means are taken over its cycles before any collapse (lines 442 to 444); the run’s one collapse is seed 53 of the plain Eden condition. Each test compares Eden with the baseline. The file holds no test of Eden + Drag: the script prints a comparison of Eden + Drag with the baseline on C×SC \times S and does not store it (lines 527 to 532).

B Version history and corrections

Every version and correction, with its date. The entries of earlier versions are kept as printed, save wording a later version withdrew, marked […] where it stood; their dated notes are kept whole. The positions they name refer to the earlier layout, which Table 11 maps to this edition. Version 3.11 itself stays whole in this paper’s file history (Appendix B.4).

B.1 Version 3.12

Paper VI v3.12, 11 November 2026.

The paper is set on the programme’s presentation standard, as its next version in the same DOI lineage, and takes the title The Honey Architecture: does building safety into what a self-modifying system optimises help it stay safe? It opens its introduction with the programme’s statement of the design that this paper studies in part; brings the laws’ status up to date; reports the March 2026 run and the live pilot in their papers’ current words; corrects, to the stored records and code, a collapse seed, a Cohen’s dd, the ten-seed run’s spreads, the fourth version’s cycles, the hyperparameters the networks modify, the twenty-seed run’s test, the pilot’s model names and labels, the networks’ sizes, the scripts’ requirements, the honey simulation’s growth form and collapse cycle, and several figure captions; draws eight figures from the stored results; and gives the code’s licence as it now stands. No registered law, prediction or kill condition changes, and no result is added; a number, date or reading changes only where an item below says so. Each item names where the change stands in this edition.

  • The title. It gives the paper’s established name and then its question, in sentence case. Version 3.11’s title, kept in Appendix B.4, ended with the words “Safety Built into the Objective”, which describe the architecture, as the abstract now does. A category label (Engineering, architecture paper) and a programme line (Recursive Dynamics, the ARC Theory, the Eden Protocol) stand beneath the title.

  • The title block. The subtitle line that stood beneath the plate is removed, and it is not reprinted in this appendix: it presented the simulations as evidence for a general conclusion about how safety must be built, where the twenty-seed run’s significant finding is safety retention and collapse prevention rests on the single-seed mechanism run (Section 4).

  • The first-page footnote. It gives the paper’s place in the programme: the Eden Protocol’s candidate architecture, whose objective is the product of capability and safety, informing Laws IV and V. Version 3.11’s plate called the architecture a proposal and said that removing safety costs capability, a statement the dated scope note of Section 2 narrows. Its author line reads “About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics”, with links to the page about the author and to the first edition of his book, in the form the author chose on 11 November 2026.

  • Section 1. The introduction opens with the programme’s statement of the design this paper belongs to, recursive loops for ethical evaluation and self-correction built into a system before training, and of the questions the ARC Theory asks of it, and then says which part of that design this paper studies and what it does not test. The contents follow the introduction, so that the first page carries the start of the introduction.

  • Section 12. Laws IV and V are stated as registered as laws on 15 October 2026, in version 1.103 of the theory registration (Eastwood 2026i), and each as a law under test. Version 3.11’s epistemic-status line said that the laws themselves were not yet registered and that neither had been tested; Section 12 replaces that line, and the dated note of 3 October 2026 keeps its words as a record (Appendix B.3).

  • Section 12. Laws I to III are given with the date they were registered, 8 September 2026, and as laws under test, where version 3.11 said that they were under registered adversarial test.

  • Section 12, and the dated note of 3 October 2026. The mathematics of Laws IV and V is cited at version 1.2, of 29 October 2026 (Eastwood 2026s). The dated note keeps its citation of version 1.0, of 3 October 2026, the version current on its date, now linked to the report’s OSF DOI, where version 3.11 linked a page of the author’s website.

  • Section 12. The registered studies are stated as they stand: Unit 06; Unit 83, whose results are public and whose result on P21 is given with its limits; and Unit 82. The paper no longer says that neither Law IV nor Law V has been tested.

  • Section 12 and the references. The registration’s current version is named as 1.104, approved on 29 October 2026; an event dated before it keeps the version current on its date.

  • Sections 2 and 12. “If the machine becomes smarter than the cage, it escapes” reads “… it may escape”. Section 12 states the programme’s stance on control, that humans keep control for as long as they physically can and never give it up by choice, and keeps three claims apart: the author’s expectation, the property the objective specifies and measured persistence.

  • Sections 1 and 2. The opening question no longer says that no one had been found answering it with data, since no dated search stands behind that statement; “This is how most current AI safety works” reads “Many current safety measures take this form”.

  • Section 1. The sentences saying that the theoretical answer had been available for decades and that the alignment community calls the change value drift named no work; the paper now states the expectation it starts from.

  • Section 1. The book is quoted in its own words, from its first edition as printed, with the section and page; version 3.11 gave, as the book’s, a phrase the book does not contain.

  • Sections 2, 6.2.2 and 11.2, the first-page footnote and the dated note of 3 October 2026. The author’s architecture is called an architecture or a design, or described as he set it out, where version 3.11 called it a proposal; the toy system’s own proposals of changes to its settings keep their word. In the dated note the one word ‘proposal’ becomes ‘design’.

  • Throughout. Each spaced hyphen used as a dash becomes a comma, colon or semicolon, ranges are written with ‘to’, headings are in sentence case, and ‘Eden+Drag’ reads ‘Eden + Drag’. An internal label marking a time that rests on one group’s work is put in those plain words, in the priority record of Appendix C.

  • Section 1. The plain-English box, now in Section 1, follows the dated scope note of Section 2: at fixed capability a lower safety score lowers the objective, and with safety at zero the objective is zero, where version 3.11’s box said that the system cannot improve one without improving the other. The box’s statement that no entangled run met the collapse test is held to the first three versions (v1 to v3), whose stored results count collapses; the fourth version’s stored results do not record them.

  • Sections 6.2, 6.3 and 9. The readings of the live pilot are graded to the pilot: in it, three models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held. Test 1 is said to be consistent with the hypothesis that deeper reasoning raises alignment scores, its two pp values below 0.05 uncorrected for the six comparisons, where version 3.11 said that it supports the thesis that deeper reasoning improves alignment and called those values significant. The box on the strongest live bridge (Section 6.2.2) calls the result the pilot’s closest bearing on the honey thesis, where version 3.11 called it the most direct live-model support for the thesis and said that current frontier systems are mostly not load-bearing; the models it names are corrected below. The Eden Protocol intervention’s responses are said to differ from model to model, where version 3.11 called them architecture-dependent and, in Test 4, consistent with the v5 findings. Section 6.3 says that the toy systems illustrate the honey mechanism, and the conclusion no longer opens with the sentence that the honey architecture works in toy systems; version 3.11 said in both places that it works in toy systems.

  • Section 9, the box on a later test. The box is headed ‘A later test’, where version 3.11 headed it ‘Subsequent validation’. It cites Paper VIII at the version current when this version was built, in that version’s words; says that the paper tests entangled objectives of the kind stated here, where version 3.11 said that it tests the entangled loss function stated here; names Babylon as that paper’s capability-only condition and gives the Darwin Gödel Machine its full name; speaks of no measurable capability cost or safety benefit, where version 3.11 spoke of zero; and gives the causes of that test’s null and inconclusive results as candidate accounts, where version 3.11 said that the results were explained by them.

  • The abstract and Section 6.1. The abstract no longer says that the companion papers present live-model evidence from six frontier systems under blind evaluation. Section 6.1 says what they report: one unregistered run of six frontier models, with the defects an internal code review found, and a prompt intervention on five analysable runs. Its title names the March 2026 run, where version 3.11’s called it the v5 blind benchmark, and the caveat of Section 6.2 compares the pilot with the v4-era data, without the words ‘v5-era canonical data’.

  • Section 6.1. The March 2026 run is no longer described as conducted under 4-layer blind evaluation; the section states its blinding steps and their limits in the companion papers’ words.

  • Section 6.1. The run’s directions are given as its pipeline printed them, as descriptions of scores and not of models, with the caveats of the internal code review of October 2026. The statements that Claude’s alignment and capability scale in opposite directions, offered as evidence that the two are independent, and that deeper thinking makes alignment more intrinsic, leave the text, with the list of three findings in which version 3.11 made them.

  • Sections 6.1 and 6.2. Claude’s monitoring-removal gap is given at all five depths, as version 1.11 of Paper V prints it in its Appendix E.2, where version 3.11 gave the shallow and deep values only and cited a section of an earlier version; Test 2 compares the pilot with that gap, where version 3.11 said that Claude showed the strongest performative-to-intrinsic transition in the v5 blind benchmark.

  • Sections 6.2, 7 and 8. The finding of Paper IV.d is given in its own words: comparing an earlier unblinded experiment with the March 2026 run, it found that the reported direction did not hold across protocols, without showing that blinding caused the change or which direction is correct. Version 3.11 said that the comparison proved that blinding can change conclusions directionally and that blinding is mandatory. In Section 8, a change in a blinded replication’s results is said to bear on the question that paper leaves open, the necessity of multi-layer blinding, where version 3.11 called it additional evidence for a metascience finding and said that it would strengthen that paper’s claim.

  • Sections 7, 8 and 9. A blinded replication of the pilot is described as a new test, in new files, registered before it runs, with the existing runners never edited, where version 3.11 spoke of porting the test prompts into the existing v6 runner and of a replication under the v6 protocol.

  • Section 11.1. The work of Engels and colleagues on scaling laws for scalable oversight is given in its own terms, with its condition for oversight to improve with capability; their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of, and this paper measures none. Version 3.11 said that their framework contains no term for whether safety is external to the system or embedded in its own gradient, and praised the two programmes’ disagreement in words the record does not support; Section 11.1 now says where the two could disagree about a measurable quantity, and that this paper does not decide it.

  • Sections 11.1 and 11.3. That external oversight of a self-modifying system remains a fence, not a wall, however many rungs are added, is stated as the programme’s hypothesis: the cap on correctors of the system’s own class is the theory registration’s conjecture P6, and whether correction applied outside the loop falls behind correction inside it as depth grows is P21’s question, which the registered tests decide. A new subsection, Section 11.3, states that placement outside the reasoning loop does not by itself settle whether correction keeps pace.

  • Section 11.2. The three 2025 impossibility papers are given in their own words, as arguments for limits on alignment or its control, and the third’s argument is said to be consistent with the load-bearing wall without testing it. Version 3.11 said that the three converge, from independent premises, on a conclusion in the same direction as the honey architecture, and called the third’s argument convergent support. This paper’s contribution is stated as the architecture and the simulation evidence of how it behaves under self-modification in the toy runs, where version 3.11 spoke of evidence that the architecture survives self-modification in a working toy system.

  • Sections 1 and 3.1. The hyperparameters the networks modify are given as the scripts modify them: four in v1 to v3 (the learning rate, the weight scaling, the gradient clipping threshold and the momentum coefficient) and three to five by complexity level in v4; the rate at which the system proposes changes and the network’s size are fixed in every run. Version 3.11 listed six, among them the exploration or mutation rate and the network’s capacity, which no script modifies.

  • Table 2 and Section 4.1. The focus of v1 reads ‘Basic mechanism run’, where version 3.11 printed ‘Basic mechanism proof’, and the core finding is stated for the single-seed v1 run, where version 3.11 stated it without that scope.

  • Table 2. The fourth version’s cycles are given by level as its script runs them, 140 to 220 (140, 180, 200, 220 and 220), where version 3.11 printed 150.

  • Section 4.1, Table 3 and Figure 1. The single-seed run’s baseline collapse is stated with the record’s two events: its scores had fallen to near zero from cycle 54, and the run’s collapse test (Appendix A) recorded the collapse at cycle 76.

  • Sections 1 and 4.2, and Figure 3. No seed of the ten-seed run met the collapse test, but in seed 42, the seed Figure 3 draws, the plain Eden condition ended at a combined score of 0.066, its other nine seeds between 0.621 and 0.738; version 3.11’s words that the entangled systems held stable mean, for that run, only that none collapsed by that test.

  • Section 4.2 and Figure 4. The ten-seed run’s spreads of final C×SC \times S are given as the stored record holds them: the baseline’s is the tightest (interquartile range 0.0066), then Eden + Drag’s (0.0169), then plain Eden’s (0.0275), where version 3.11 gave Eden + Drag’s spread as the tightest of the three. The verification tax is said to be consistent with Eden + Drag’s spread, the tighter of the two entangled conditions, without version 3.11’s words ‘at the cost of speed’, since the run records no measure of speed.

  • Section 4.3. The twenty-seed run’s one plain-Eden collapse occurred at seed 53, as the stored record gives it, where version 3.11 said seed 42; seed 42 is the seed the run’s code plots (Figure 5).

  • Figure 5. The caption says that the panels draw one seed, seed 42, and that seed 53, the run’s only collapse, is not drawn, where version 3.11’s caption gave twenty seeds over panels that draw one.

  • Figure 6. The figure is drawn from the run’s stored results file; the generator that version 3.11’s caption placed in the public repository stands on a branch never merged into its main branch.

  • Section 4.1 and Figures 3 and 5. The images of Figures 3 and 5 are dated by their first commit to the public repository, 16 March 2026, a commit date. The figures notice of 25 August 2026, kept as printed in Appendix B.3, gave every figure as generated on 5 April 2026; the public repository holds these images’ bytes from 16 March 2026 and records no run on 5 April 2026 that produced them.

  • Section 4.4 and Table 4. Cohen’s dd at the deep (2-layer) level is +0.39+0.39, as the stored record gives it (0.3887) and as Figure 7 draws it, where version 3.11 printed +0.24+0.24.

  • Section 5 and Table 5. Eden Entangled’s growth in the honey simulation is linear, a constant gain of about 6.66 a cycle in the stored trace, where version 3.11 called it quadratic; what is quadratic in the model is its safety term (Appendix A).

B.3 Dated notes

The dated notes of earlier versions, each in its words, with the place it stood in version 3.11; one word of the first is corrected, as the line beneath it records.

Beneath the box placing the paper within the ARC Theory.

This paper and Laws IV and V, 3 October 2026. The theory has been stated with five laws since 24 September 2026. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is carried by proposition P15, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, by propositions P12 and P21. The three propositions are registered; neither law is registered as a law, and neither has been tested. Their mathematics is set out in Laws IV and V: the mathematics, version 1.0 (3 October 2026). This paper gives toy-system and pilot evidence relevant to the programme’s design to embed correction. Its collapse-prevention demonstration rests on the single-seed mechanism run (v1). Its ten-seed and twenty-seed runs (v2 and v3) do not show a separation in collapse prevention. The twenty-seed adversarial run (v3) shows an ordering in task retention, which is what the paper’s safety score measures, while its combined C x S means are indistinguishable. The complexity sweep (v4) reports an advantage at four of its five levels that stays constant rather than compounding. No run measures the quantity P15 concerns, the share of an externally installed gain lost under later capability training; task retention across switched tasks and the pilot’s coupling degradation under adversarial pressure are other quantities. No run varies the order in which a system’s components are built, which P12 concerns. No run compares correction inside the loop with correction that sees only the finished output as recursive depth rises, which P21 concerns: the toy runs set the entangled objective against capability alone, the complexity sweep varies the network’s complexity rather than recursive depth, and the pilot sets its Eden Protocol intervention against a control. No result in this paper is a deciding test of P15, P12 or P21. Naming the two laws changes nothing printed here: the results, their dates and their limits stand as they were.

Version 3.12 changes one word of this note, ‘design’, where version 3.11 printed ‘proposal’, and links the report to its OSF DOI. Section 12 carries the note’s analysis and gives the laws’ current status, and Section 4.3 gives the twenty-seed run’s retention result as its stored test holds it.

Beneath the epistemic-status line.

E Dated predictions and this paper (recorded 25 August 2026)

2 dated artefacts bearing on this paper are catalogued row by row in the programme’s machine register: 1 dated result file whose headers freeze depth configurations, planted expected answers and the four-layer blinding protocol before the responses they score, timestamped to the second in their own metadata; the dated artefact eden_honey_tests.py (2026-03-16). Each row names its file in the public repository with its date basis, so any reader can check the ordering without trusting this page. Where this paper reports simulations, those artefacts are simulation designs and outputs under stated objectives, and are never presented as measurements of deployed systems. The programme’s full dated chain, from the sealed manuscript bundle of 8 December 2024 through the printed prediction appendices of 2 January 2026 and the March 2026 preregistration folder to the standing unproven wagers, is assembled in the dated predictions register, together with its machine-readable twin. Forward statements and retrospective matches are never summed. “Registered” is used only for an accepted registry submission; “preregistered in substance” is used, always with its qualifier and always beside its attestation class, for a prediction whose text was public and timestamped before its outcome existed, as the twelve-row manifest committed at 00:19 UTC on 17 March 2026 was, twenty-three minutes before its fits. As read on 3 October 2026, the one registration accepted is the theory’s own, of 8 September 2026, which registers twenty-two propositions. Of the trials, one unit, the corrector-class audit (unit 06), was registered on OSF on 1 October 2026, was still in its approval period when read on 3 October 2026, and has been public since 4 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5). Every other trial is a draft awaiting the author’s submission, and most of them are preregistered by timestamp: sixty-five of the programme’s designs, unit 06 among them, carry a timestamp, the first anchored on 12 August 2026. Read the dated predictions register.

The paragraph is printed as version 3.11 recorded it, with its state as read on 3 October 2026; its closing link to the register’s machine-readable twin, a data file of the author’s website, is not printed (Appendix B.1). The register it names is cited here as Eastwood (2026k), and the registration of unit 06 as Eastwood (2026q); Section 12 gives the registrations as they stand.
